subtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT OF RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT OF RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext:
I wish to ask the Prime Minister
whether, in connection with the reference which I understand is being made to the Supreme Court of Canada regarding the jurisdiction of the tariff board, the government will consider referring the question as to the validity of orders fixing values for duty purposes of commodities covered by the British preference since the statute of 1932 was passed?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT OF RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext:
As far as I know that question
has not been raised. The questions raised were: First, has the board any jurisdiction to settle or determine questions of law; second, was the judgment of the board in connection with the matter of the refund of duty in connection with twine under a valuation fixed by the minister under the authority of an order in council passed prior to the enactment of the statute providing that section 43 did not apply to British Empire countries valid or invalid? The third question, which has just been mentioned by the hon. gentleman, has not arisen so far as I know. It has not been determined that the matter should be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada; the law officers are endeavouring to ascertain just what would be the appropriate method, apart altogether from resorting to the rather cumbersome proceeding provided by the Customs Act, to have the matter speedily disposed of. That matter will be settled by to-morrow.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT OF RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext: In that connection might I just remind the Prime Minister that there would seem to be two more questions. One is allied to the second question he mentioned; that is, whether or not orders made by the minister after the passing of the statute of 1932 are valid. The second question is as to whether the privy council have any power to entertain an appeal under section 54 in respect of questions such as were raised in the twine case. I just wanted to ask if the government will consider putting those questions in the reference, if such a reference is proposed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT OF RIGHT TO MAKE RULINGS ON POINTS OF LAW AND FIXING OF VALUES
speechtext: With your consent, Mr. Speaker, I desire to say that the government is not in a position to make a reference other than with respect to the matters that were raised on the appeal, and when the appeal was presented it was admitted that, for the purpose of discussion, there was an appeal under the section to which reference has been made.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I was going to ask the hon.
gentleman if he would be good enough to wait another day. The letter to which I referred is not on file; this subject matter was dealt with in a verbal statement, and I have asked that a letter be sent to show that the moneys received have been used for the purpose of liquidating the obligations mentioned in the order in council. I have telephoned again to have the letter sent. There are no communications between the railway company and the government.
On the orders of the day:

I
should like to direct a question to the acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau) and also to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. MacLaren), because both departments are involved. My question is in connection with an article which appeared in L'Aetion Catholique, of Quebec, on Tuesday, March 6, 1934, as follows:
(Translation)
Inedible fish. We have been informed that, recently, fish practically rotten has been sold in Quebec. Is it necessary to condemn such a practice? WTe trust that the authorities will take the matter up with the owners of cold storage warehouses as soon as they learn the facts.

Supply-Defence-Naval Services
Then an advertisement:
Eels for sale at the cold storage warehouse of the Quebec commission.
I am informed that the fish referred to are a consignment of eels which are being sold for 3 cents a pound either by or from the Quebec cold storage warehouse. The question I should like to ask the acting Minister of Fisheries is whether he will inquire as to whether or not these inedible fish are being sold from this warehouse, and the question I should like to ask the Minister of Pensions and National Health is whether he will take steps to see that fish unfit for food are not sold in Quebec.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Eels are a great delicacy in Holland.

That may be so; I did not want to detain the house at any length, but the house will remember what was contained in the advertisement.
Eels, not graded, at $3 per hundredweight, with a reduction of 10 per cent in quantities of five boxes or more. A box contains from 100 to 150 pounds.
The article I read is to the effect that fish unfit for human consumption are being sold in the city of Quebec. I do not place eels in the category of unfit food, but bad eels or, as it is expressed here, rotten eels certainly are not in the category of food fit for consumption, even in the city of Quebec.

speakeroldname: Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Acting Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: This is the first time I have heard of these facts. I shall be pleased to inquire into the matter as far as it comes under the jurisdiction of my department, but I think these questions should be addressed to the provincial and municipal authorities.

In all probability they
should be, but we will start here.

speakeroldname: Hon. MURRAY MacLAREN (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I should be glad if my hon. friend would hand me the statements to which he has referred, and I shall have inquiries made at once in reference thereto.
On the orders of the day:
I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) if it is intended to bring in any amendments to the Seed Act this session.
Not in connection with the administration of the Seed Act, so far as I am aware.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Gagnon in the chair.
Militia services: permanent force, $4,910,034.

I should like to ask the minister a question, though I am not sure whether or not this is the proper item. It is in connection with the sale of the rifle range on Lulu island in British Columbia. Has the range been sold and, if so, was it sold by tender?
Hon. DONALD M. SUTHERLAND (Minister of National Defence):	No, it has not
been sold.

Have
tenders been called for the sale of the range?
No.

Item agreed to.
Naval services-to provide for the maintenance of the ships and establishments of the naval service, including the Royal Canadian Navy, the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve and the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve, $2,222,000.

May I
ask where the saving of $200,000 has been effected under this item?

The savings have
been effected entirely with regard to supplies. We will not buy as many supplies as heretofore.

On this item I should like to join with the remarks of the minister last night concerning Commodore Hose. In view of the long connection of that officer with the naval service I believe it is fitting that those of us who knew something about his good qualities should record our appreciation of the service he rendered to this country. I must say that during my term in office I found him to be a most efficient, loyal and capable officer, and one whose services bore out in an extremely fine manner the best traditions of the British naval service.
Would the minister tell me the names of the members of the defence council?

The minister, of
course, is president, and the deputy minister vice-president. Then there is General Mc-Naughton chief of general staff; Brigadier Constantine, adjutant general, and Brigadier Caldwell, quartermaster general. In the meantime the associate members are the acting chief of the naval service, Captain Nelles, and Group Captain Croil of the air force.

Supply-Defence-Naval Services

Could the minister give
me the salaries and allowances of these members of the defence council?
I presume you want to know my salary?
No, we do not want that.
The chief of general staff receives $10,000; Brigadier Constantine, $7,500; Brigadier Caldwell, $7,500; Captain Nelles, $7,250 and Group Captain Croil, $5,800.

Do any of these officers
get any other allowances from the public service, in addition to these amounts?
No; allowances are included in every case.

Following the question
asked by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, may I ask as to whether or not the chief of general staff has any Jurisdiction over the acting chief of the naval staff?

None whatever. Of course I have to amplify that statement a little bit. As the hon. gentleman did, we are endeavouring to correlate activities and to have all people working together. The situation as regards the naval service is exactly the same in every particular as it was when the hon. member was in office.
While we are on this subject would the minister permit me to ask if his statement holds true with respect to the air force, also?

No, it is not exactly the same as obtains in the air force. When the hon. gentleman was in office the civil government air operations reported through the deputy minister. At the present time they report through the general staff. The chief of civil aviation, Mr. Wilson, reports through the deputy minister.

Does the chief of the
Royal Canadian Air Force report direct to the deputy minister?

No, he reports
through the chief of the general staff.

How long has the system mentioned by the minister been in operation, first as to the chief of the civil aviation branch reporting to the chief of general staff and secondly the chief of the Royal Canadian Air Force reporting to the chief of general staff?

Formerly there were, more or less, two departments, namely the Royal Canadian Air Force and civil government operations. For some time past they have been run as one. In other times the

air force reported through the chief of general staff.

If the minister carries out what I hope he proposes to do, and what I believe he proposes to do, namely, to increase activities of civil government operations, does he not think it would be better to have civil government operations reporting directly to the deputy minister?
That will have to be considered. I would not be in a position, really, to answer that question.

When was the change
made? '
I think the change was made in the estimates two years ago. At that time both operations were in one estimate.
No, they are still under separate votes.

They are at this
time; they were brought in in that way for purposes of clarification. But last year and the year before I think the hon. member will find that they appeared as one vote.

I would hope that the line of communication and the chain of responsibility would follow the votes as indicated in numbers 82 and 83 of the estimates we are now discussing, and that at least civil aviation should report directly to the deputy minister. It seems to me it is a distinct branch.
Civil aviation does that.
I must have misunderstood the minister. I understood him to say that they reported to the chief of general staff.
No; Mr. Wilson reports directly to the deputy minister.

I misunderstood the minister. The position is that the chief of the Royal Canadian Air Force reports to the chief of the general staff but the head of the civil aviation branch, Mr. Wilson, reports to the deputy minister?
Yes.

I should -like to have some information in regard to item 79, naval, services. This vote is "to provide for the maintenance of the ships and establishments of the naval service, including the Royal Canadian Navy, the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve and the Royal Canadian Naval

Supply-Defence-Naval Services
Volunteer Reserve." I wonder if the minister would be good enough to tell the committee how many ships there are, and something about them. This is a large vote of over $2,000,000.

We have the
Saguenay, which is a destroyer on the eastern coast, and the Skeena, another destroyer on the western coast. These two boats are new, and were bought only recently.
At what cost?
About $3,000,000 for the two of them.
From whom were they purchased?

They were purchased in England, from Thornycroft's. Then, we have the Champlain and the Vancouver, which although older destroyers are in very good condition. Then there are two mine layers, the Festubert and the Armentieres. The first is at Halifax and the second at Esquimalt.
What is the tonnage of those destroyers and their operation costs per day?

The expenses for the year are:	Saguenay, $256,000, Champlain,
$190,000, Festubert, $41,000, Skeena, $252,000, Vancouver, $183,000, Armentieres, $41,000.
What is the total personnel of the naval forces?
The total is 864.
The figures the minister has just given as the expenses in connection with the boats represent the cost for the year?
Yes.

The minister was kind enough to inform me last year that the expenses per day for the Saguenay were $645, and that the Saguenay is in operation all the year around; and that the maintenance and service of the Champlain cost per day $485. I understand that the cost would be approximately the same for the Vancouver and the Skeena. Would the minister state if the amounts I have just mentioned are correct?
If they were the amounts I gave the hon. gentleman last year I have no doubt at all that they are correct.
Would the minister be kind enough to inform the committee how many Canadians have attended the lectures at the Empire State college in England?

As the hon. gentleman knows, by agreement we send officers every year to take advanced training courses in naval matters in England. During the present year there will be one officer taking the staff course at Greenwich, two officers taking the technical course on naval matters, and two officers taking another course on technical matters. In addition the young cadets who enter the navy get their training in England. There will be six cadets going over.
Mr. POTJiLIOT: But I am asking how many Canadians have attended the lectures at that college.
Ever since the institution of our navy, following the war.
Ever since the war.
Oh, yes.
Does Canada pay their expenses over there?
Yes.
Is the Empire State college a kind of English West Point? Is it England's equivalent to West Point in the United States?

No. West Point, of course, is for the military service only and corresponds more to our Royal Military college. The institution in England to which the hon. gentleman refers, and to which we send cadets, is the training ship Frobisher. That is where our midshipmen go.
If I understand the minister correctly, it is a naval school.
Yes.
Besides that are there lectures given on air force matters and airways?

Not at that particular school. But there is in the old country what is called the Imperial Defence college to which officers from all over the empire go to discuss and be instructed in the higher elements of military, naval and aerial affairs. The senior officers in Great Britain from all the great services come and address and instruct and give lectures to those who are attending those courses.

Would the minister be
kind enough to tell the committee the name of that school or college and where it is located?

It is called the
Imperial Defence college and is located in London.
1552	COMMONS
Supply-Defence-Naval Services
Mr. PO'ULIOT:	How long has it been in
existence?
It is an old-established institution, not a recent thing at all. I am not aware of the exact year in which it was established.

Would the minister be
kind enough to tell the house for how long Canadians have been attending that school?
I am not in a position to say just how long, but I believe they have been attending it for a great many years.

More than three or four
years?
Oh, yes, more than that.
How old are the boys or the men who attend that college?

Of course, the ones
who go from Canada are senior officers who have gone as far as they could in this country. There are no boys or junior officers attending that school.

I thank the minister for
his very valuable information. My own idea is that when a man is a pupil after twenty-five years of age he will remain in infancy all his life. Of course, a man must study all his life, but there is a great difference between a pupil and a man who studies. I do not see why Canadians should go to that pompously named institution in London in order to be taught imperialism. I believe in Canadianism. We have strong ties with the British Empire but we have no lessons to receive in love of our country. All Canadians love their country and they must love it before any other. I admit that our ties with Great Britain are strong and that our king is the king of Great Britain, but on the other hand Canadians should be taught first to be good, real Canadians, and Canadians before anything else. I protest strongly against sending Canadians to be taught imperialism in London or anywhere else. I regret that these peregrinations take place, and I hope that the minister will see to it that if these men go there in order to receive technical training they will be taught nothing else but technical matters about the naval service, the air service and so on. They should not be taught that they must love England before Canada.

A few moments ago
the minister, replying to a question of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, gave the total personnel of the naval forces as 800 odd. Does that include the personnel of the naval reserve and of the naval volunteer reserve?
I may have inadvertently misled the committee. That was the number of the permanent force, men on the strength all the time.

What is the strength
of the naval reserve and of the naval volunteer reserve?

The personnel of
the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve is 1,028. That corresponds in the naval service with our non-permanent militia coming under the militia vote. Then we have 200 in the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve.
Could the minister give me the strength of the naval volunteer reserve and where they are trained?

As I indicated
before, this body corresponds to the nonpermanent militia. They are situated at Calgary, Charlottetown, Edmonton, Halifax, Montreal, Ottawa, Prince Rupert, Quebec, Regina, Saint John, Saskatoon, Toronto, Vancouver and Winnipeg.
Do they draw pay and allowances?
They draw pay and allowances. From time to time certain complements go to the coast for actual training on board one of the destroyers.
Has the efficiency of the service been affected by the reduction of $200,000 in the vote?
There has been no reduction in personnel.
Any reduction in the service?
No reduction in the service.

I wonder if the minister read the dispatch which appeared in the Citizen of Monday. This reads:
Port of Spain, Trinidad, March 11.- Canada's naval squadron has gained another victory.
In the famous Chaguaramus bay where fleeing Spaniards fired their fleet and sank their treasure cargoes in 60 fathoms of water to save them from their British pursuers, the four Canadian destroyers put to rout the British cruiser H.M.S. Dragon in mimic warfare.
The Dragon knifed its way through the water at 30 knots an hour in an effort to evade the deadly markmanship displayed during the Canadian torpedo attack.
In another manoeuvre when darkness fell across the bay, the Canadian destroyer Vancouver with all lights out, played hide-and-seek with the Saguenay, Skeena and

Supply-Defence-Air Force
Champlain as the offensive ships. The three destroyers combed the darkness and suddenly "star shells" turned night into day, revealing the Vancouver vainly pretending to be a rocky headland of the wooded island. Crew of the Vancouver were eating supper in darkness when the shells from the other destroyers disclosed their position.
Later the Canadian tars showed their prowess as "excellent" gunners, submerging every floating target with a barrage that reechoed from the mountains and cliffs of the historic Spanish Main.
I read this article simply as a protest against the manner in which public money is being wasted. The minister has told me that it costs this country something like $2,200 per day to keep these four destroyers in operation. In times of prosperity perhaps these games of hide-and-seek might be tolerated but during a time of crisis when the people are suffering hardships I think such games should cease altogether. I am speaking only for myself when I say that I believe the country could be saved a vast amount of money if the department would sell these four destroyers for whatever they would bring. I believe to spend $2,200 per day in order to allow these gentlemen to cruise in the West Indies is a waste of public money which should not be tolerated any further.

I should like to say a word or two to correct an impression which seems to exist in connection with the cruises in the south during the winter. It would be impossible for these ships to go to sea in our northern waters and it is almost imperative to follow the practice which has been followed for some time and send these ships to warmer waters during the cold months. They are able to take advantage of the fact that the northern Atlantic squadron is there also. They have an opportunity of perfecting themselves in naval manoeuvres and execution. It was decided some time ago that we should have some naval strength in this country and as long as we have that strength, these vessels must carry on training manoeuvres.

Item agreed to.
Royal Canadian Air Force-expenses in connection with the general maintenance and training of the permanent and non-permanent active air force, and provision of facilities therefor, $1,805,000.
Could the minister tell us if any new aircraft have been purchased?
No.

Are the Siskins still in
operation?
Yes.

Is all the training being
carried on at Trenton or is there some still being carried on at Camp Borden?

There is some at
Camp Borden.

Could the minister give
me the division of activities between the two places?

We are moving from Camp Borden to Trenton as fast as conditions warrant. Last year facilities were provided at Camp Borden for aib initio flying, defence flying, specialized training of the Royal Canadian Air Force personnel and training of civil pilots. Last year at Trenton there was the nucleus of one fighter and one army cooperation squadron. There is no training carried on there except the training of these squadrons.
'Could the minister explain the increase of $400,000?

It will be necessary to say a general word about that. I think most hon. members will agree that the air force estimates have -been reduced most drastically during the last three or four years since I have been head of the department. Two years ago we had to let out quite a large number of the personnel to make the vote possible. Since then the vote was reduced again and everyone concerned was of the opinion that it would be a very false move to let out any further personnel. Consequently there was not really enough money in the last vote to get the full benefit of the air force as we had it. We had too much personnel for the amount of money-that is, to allow them to fly. As a matter of fact they were grounded too much, as the expression is, and it must be realized that, granted that we are to have an air force, we must have more money for them to operate. There will be some new planes purchased, and everything that goes with them in the way of apparatus and equipment to assist in the training.
With regard to the purchase of new equipment, can the minister tell me what he has in mind? Is it something in the way of light training craft?

No. The present
idea is to buy six aircraft of a type suitable for advanced training, and they will probably be bought in England.
What type?

I am told that it
is the type under consideration.
Supply-Defence-Air Force
I do not want the minister to give away the order, because I suppose he expects some competition.

There cannot really
be very much competition in a matter of this kind, because the specifications for one aircraft are different from those of another, but the officials have been going into the matter with the idea of getting an airplane which will be most suitable to our needs from every standpoint for training purposes, bombing, photography, machine gun work and so on, to enable instruction to be given along these lines to the best advantage.
Does the minister think he will find any combination which will serve for bombing, photography and fighting as well?

The hon. gentleman is probably more expert than I am; I have to depend on the officials, and it is along that line that they are working, to secure a plane which can be put to the most advantageous use.
Will six be the limit he expects to buy?
That is what we have in mind at the present time.
What is the estimate?
The amount for the new aircraft item is $80,000.
Can the minister give me a summary of the usable aircraft now on hand in the R.C.A.F.?

There are now
ninety-nine in active use and in immediate reserve there are thirty-four, in reserve fifty-eight, or one hundred and ninety-one altogether.
The minister said something about ninety-nine being in active use.
Yes.
Can he give me some particulars, dividing them into training aircraft and fighting craft, bombers?

In what is called the fighter flight there are five Siskins active and two in reserve, and in the cooperation flight there are two active. In No. 4 squadron there are seven active and four in immediate reserve, and in No. 5 squadron there are eight active and one in reserve.

Are those all cooperation
planes?
Cooperation planes?
I thought the minister referred to them as army cooperation planes?
Yes; they are in the army cooperation flight.
As regards the two squadrons the minister has mentioned, do they come within the classification he has just read?
It is No. 4 squadron.
What about the ninetynine in active use?
At the Royal Canadian Air Force station in Ottawa there are fourteen active and ten in reserve.
Are there many Fairchilds in that?

There are one Fairchild 51 and five Fairchilds 71.
Mr. RALSTON. How are the ninety-nine made up?

At the Royal Canadian Air Force station in Winnipeg there are one Fairchild 51; one Moth 60; one Moth 80; two Fairchilds 71 and one in immediate reserve. At Borden there are eleven in active use and three A flight, seven B flight and seven in active reserve.
What about Trenton?

What I read last
refers to what is called the training group; I am told by my officials that it includes Borden and Trenton.
What make of planes does B flight include?
B flight includes two Avros, three Fairchilds F.C.W.W.; two Fairchilds 71.
How old are the Avros?

None has been
bought since I have been in the department.
They are vary old?
Yes.

The ex-air force men in
Toronto have been trying to form a volunteer squadron. Has any progress been made in aiding them?

Yes. There is a
squadron authorized and formed now in Toronto. The squadron leader is G. S. O'Brien and we hope this year to be able to give them some training.
Item agreed to-

Supply-Defence-Civil Aviation
Civil aviation-expenses in connection with the control of civil aviation, airways and airports, government and public airports and grants to airplane clubs, $187,000.
Will the minister tell us generally how that vote is made up? I notice the airplane clubs still get a grant.

It is as follows:
Controllers of civil aviation	$ 60,851
St. Hubert airdrome	 27,790
Airplane clubs and aviation schools.. 24,000 Airways and airports	 74,359
Total	$ 187,000
Are there any grants at all from the department for mail services?
No, they are altogether under the Post Office Department.
Perhaps the minister as a member of council will tell me if they are in the Post Office vote?
Yes, they are.

I suppose this is where the minister would hope to make the increase when the time comes to add to civil aviation activities; and here it seems to me is where a lot of useful service might be done. I again urge on the minister, because I think this is the appropriate place, that favourable consideration be given to an increase of activities in connection with civil aviation. I think Canadian citizens generally have shown remarkable interest in aviation matters. Years ago cities and municipalities did a lot towards constructing airports, giving us the nucleus for the chain of landing fields which are now being constructed. As I said last night, we already had a mail service established across the easier part of Canada, that is across the western prairies, and service had been given over the route now being covered by the construction of the air fields through northern Ontario. Aviation has entered largely into the development of our north country. I feel that aviation is still in the experimental stage to a degree that makes it necessary for the government to take considerable interest in civil aviation activities. I presume the minister's policy is the same as that of those who preceded him, that is not to carry on commercial aviation beyond the point of exploration and experimentation in order to furnish information to those engaged in civil aviation, and to provide at least some personnel able to take the initiative and form the nucleus of a group engaged in civil aviation in Canada. I hope that will continue to be the policy; I am not one of those
who believe in government going wholesale into civil aviation or other commercial activities, but I want to impress upon the minister and the government the great desirability of encouraging aviation in Canada by increasing as far as possible air mail services and giving contracts directly to the organizations that are in a position to carry out air mail services; also in order to provide employment for civil aviators and to encourage the whole field of aeronautical development. I think the government can do a great deal in that respect, and I would hope that some air mail services which have been abandoned may be reinstated, not only for the purposes of air mail, but for the purpose of developing aviation generally in view of what it means to the future of Canada.
What air mail services are being carried on at the present time in Canada?

These are the services: Montreal-Albany; Narrow Lake-Sioux Lookout; Winnipeg-Pembina; McMurray-Aklavik; Bissett-Lac du Bonnet; Peace River-North Vermilion; Big River-Ile a la Crosse; Resolution-Great Bear Lake; Prince Albert-Lac la Ronge; Amos to Siscoe, and summer services: Rimouski-Montreal and Vancouver-Victoria.
Winter services only:	Leamington-Pelee
island; Quebec-Seven Islands; Seven Islands-Anticosti; Moncton-Charlottetown; Charlotte-town-Magdalen islands.
Will the minister inform the committee how many air mail routes were cancelled at the time reductions were made?
I cannot tell that, because it is not under this department, but under the Post Office Department. The route from Winnipeg to Lethbridge and up to Edmonton and Calgary was the major cancellation.

Are government airplanes
used in transporting geological survey parties in the northern part of Canada, when parties are sent out by the department?
Yes, they would be our planes.
If the Department of Mines should be persuaded to do some more geological work would the air mail force now existing be quite sufficient for any work of that nature?

The services needing the help of aviation operations have a com-

Supply-Defence-Civil Aviation
mittee that try to work together and select the services which are the most important and pressing, and we try to do their work.

The government
never has assumed the responsibility of building aerodromes for municipalities. From the beginning we have regarded that as entirely a municipal duty. But we have always been ready to assist with engineering and expert knowledge. If it is an important aerodrome that will probably be used at night we would assist them to a certain extent in the ground lighting facilities.
A few minutes ago the minister gave a list of air mail services. Are there any government airplanes engaged in those services or are they all under contract with companies?
They would all be under contract with the exception of the Montreal-Rimouski service, which in the last year or so has been flown by our planes.

In view of further development of air mail services from coast to coast are any negotiations going on between the Department of National Defence and the Post Office Department as to how this scheme should be carried out? Is a policy being considered of having that service carried out by the Department of National Defence or entirely by contract with private companies?

That question has
received a great deal of close attention by a committee on which the Post Office Department has been represented. They have gone a long way, in fact as far as they can without some money to spend; they have not made any definite recommendation as to whether the larger services, when inaugurated, should be flown by the government or by a private company. There has been no decision arrived at in that regard.
Can the minister tell us the cost of the summer service between Rimouski and Montreal, undertaken by the Department of National Defence? How much per mile?
I doubt very much if I am in a position to tell that, because it was our own machines that were engaged in that service and I do not think it has been figured in that way, so far as I have it here.

Can the minister say why
the change was made from a private company to the Department of National Defence?

The contract was
cancelled purely for financial reasons; the Post Office Department did not have the money with which to carry it on. Then on more mature consideration being given, this was regarded as a very important link in the air mail service, bringing the mail from the ships at Rimouski up to Montreal and vice versa, and it was then considered that we had plenty of airplanes and plenty of pilots and that they could do that work.

I congratulate the
minister on the action he has taken. The service is carried on better, the pilots are better qualified and the air mail service is better looked after.

Since I was at the head of the Post Office Department when that service was inaugurated, I think in 1928, I was glad to learn that it is the intention of the government to maintain that service. In the initial stages it was somewhat difficult to give the service that we desired, but as years rolled by and improvements took place in air transportation we were able to give a veiy efficient service between Rimouski and Montreal by 1930.
I have yet to be convinced that the service can be more efficiently operated by the Department of National Defence than by a private company. As I understood the minister a few moments ago the change to the Department of National Defence was not made on grounds of efficiency but on grounds of economy. When it was initiated the service cost about $1.25 per mile under contract with a private company. No doubt air mail service which in 1928 or 1930 cost all the way from 90 cents to $1.25 a mile according to the district covered could be furnished to-day for a great deal less, and with all the red tape that surrounds matters pertaining to national defence I doubt whether the department can do that work at a lower cost than would be charged by private companies. I regret that the minister is not in a position

to give me the cost per mile and the poundage of mail matter carried since the Department of National Defence took over the service from Rimouski to Montreal. I am sure that if those figures could be obtained it would be found that the work could be done more cheaply under private contract than it is being done by the department. I have no fault to find with any of the services being carried on by the department, because I know nothing about them, but I do know something about the mail service.
I must say here, Mr. Chairman, that I very much regret that the government has seen fit to do away with many of the air mail services which were established during my time as Postmaster General. Economy was given as the reason why certain services were abandoned, but I think if care had been taken in the carrying on of those services, with the yearly increases in poundage and in revenue which were then taking place, and especially with the revenue from first class matter increased through an increase in postage from 2 cents to 3 cents per ounce in certain districts and from 5 to 6 cents in others, if those services had been continued, it would have been discovered that they would have been brought up almost to a paying basis. In 1931 the 2 cent air mail service which was given to districts inaccessible by any other means, such as newly developed mining districts, the Mackenzie river district up to Aklavik, the Anticosti island district and the Magdalen island district in winter time, showed a surplus of revenue over expenditure of $169,000. The five cent service from Saint John to Montreal, it is true, was not paying; there was a deficit. The service from Montreal to New York was almost at the point where it was paying expenses. The service from Toronto to certain sections of the United States was bringing in more revenue each year, and there was a clause in the contracts with these private companies providing that on one month's notice the contracts could be changed and new arrangements entered into. It was contemplated that the rate, which varied from 90 cents to $1.20 a mile, could be reduced somewhat due to lower costs of operation, and at that time the department was about to open negotiations looking to better arrangements under these contracts. The total deficit, including that for the services in the western provinces, was in the vicinity of $750,000 annually, less the surplus of $169,000 which I have mentioned. With increased revenues resulting from greater development in the western provinces and with increased revenues on the services between Halifax and Montreal, Montreal and New
York and Montreal and Toronto, that deficit would have been reduced by something like $250,000 to $300,000 by 1932.
So I say it is a pity, Mr. Chairman, especially now that there is talk of trans-Atlantic and even trans-Pacific air mail services, that these links which were giving satisfaction and which it was intended to extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific, have been discontinued. Had these been in operation to-day Canada would have been placed in a premier position in connection with air mail transportation, since we would have had a service by means of which mail could be transported from the Atlantic to the Pacific in some eighty to ninety hours instead of taking from five to six days. I regret very much that the government has cut the principal services to such an extent; I do hope that in the negotiations which I understand have been undertaken recently the government will see its way clear to the establishment of a trans-continental service from the Atlantic to the Pacific, that that service will not be combined with the railway service of Canada, and that the air mail service shall be distinct and apart from the Canadian railway system. We have companies in Canada big enough and financially strong enough to undertake that service, without the necessity of combining with the railway services. The railway mail service is costing Canada between $7,000,000 and $8,000,000 yearly, and while it is efficient, I believe the mail service could be made more efficient by the addition of air mail facilities. That addition should not in any respect interfere with the railway mail service operating to-day. I hope that when the government reach the point where they are in a position to decide as to the reestablishment of these routes, they will do so. I am speaking from the viewpoint of encouraging civil air service in Canada. As the exMinister of National Defence said a while ago we would not have our present air service in Canada had it not been for the fact that the Post Office Department stepped into the breach in 1927 and 1928 and inaugurated a system of air mails. At that time the air mail service formed the nucleus for commercial air services carried on in Canada.
I hope that in the very near future the government will make up its mind that the day has come when Canada should have an air mail service stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

In none of these other

Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) in connection with the agricultural interests of Ontario and Quebec. I also deplored the large reductions made each year by the hon. minister in the agricultural budget. I was commenting on the item referring to cheese which the committee is at present considering. When the Imperial Economic agreements were discussed and approved in Ottawa in 1932, the government considered that they had made a great advance towards improving the situation of our farmers. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) took the pains in his speech to refer especially to cheese, pointing out the importance he attached to these so-called concessions from the United Kingdom in connection with our cheese exports. On October 10, 1932, he expressed himself in the house as follows:
Canada will enjoy in the British market free entry for three years, with preference margin of 15 per cent which will be maintained during the currency of the agreement.
Not only, sir, did this treaty not attain the object sought, but we note that cheese exports are yearly decreasing and that instead of occupying the first place, Canada has dropped to-day to the fourth place in this respect. That is why the bulletin of the bureau of statistics on October 17, 1933, published the following statement:
Within the last twelve months cheese exports have been much less than those of the previous year.

states:

Before proceeding with my remarks on the subject, may I, sir, remind the house of a statement made by the hon. Minister of Agriculture. On May 10, 1932, referring to the dairy industry he expressed himself as follows:
So I think if we were to concentrate on dairy products we should concentrate on cheese. . . .
It is unfortunate that the hon. Minister of Agriculture limited his effort to this suggestion. His inertia has caused our exports to considerably decrease and, as I stated a moment ago, instead of occupying the first place on the British market, as a cheese exporting country, we have dropped, to-day, to the fourth place. That is an unfortunate result of the Imperial Economic Conference agreements, at Ottawa, in 1932.
During the last election campaign in the constituency which I have the honour of representing, I well remember that it was difficult, if not impossible, to force the Conservative candidate to discuss any other subject but butter. Although the fanners were obtaining a profitable price for that commodity, from 1922 to 1930, the Conservative candidate promised that, should the Con-[Mr. G'rouardJ
servative party assume power, butter imports would be entirely shut out and predicted very profitable prices.
Previous to quoting figures on butter imports, sir, may I point out that it is very difficult to obtain information in this respect. Ever since the Bureau of Statistics has become a kind of advertising agency for the government's policy-and this, I am quite sure contrary to the wishes of Mr. Coats, who is an expert in this connection-it is difficult to obtain reliable statistics. Those that are at our disposal are incomplete and, at times, contradictory. However, I have done my best to gather statistics which seem to 'be most reliable and reveal the true situation. From October 1, 1930 to April 30, 1931, the government has permitted the importation of 5,031,419 pounds of butter; out of this quantity,
2 147.494 pounds were imported from February 1, 1931, to April 30, 1931. In 1032, our butter imports amounted to 879,670 pounds; in 1933, 1,377,137 pounds. I was almost forgetting 1931. It was the year which immediately followed the election, in the course of which my opponent had promised the farmers that butter imports would absolutely cease, that butter would not be allowed to enter Canada, that the government would raise the tariff sufficiently so as to bring about higher prices than those prevailing in August, 1930. Would you be amazed, sir, if I informed you that, for 1931, we imported into this country 16,500,801 pounds of butter? These figures are not included in the statistics which the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) or the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) gave to the house; however, I find these figures in the Canada Year Book, 1933, at page 565. The hon. Minister of Agriculture will note that, for the year 1931 alone, we imported 16,500,801 pounds of butter.
The calendar year or fiscal year?
The university year!
The Canada Year Book, 1933, page 565.
The calendar year?

The
university year!

It must be the calendar year. I refer the hon. member to the 'Canada Year Book, 1933, page 565.
I have no information about our butter imports for the year 1934 up to date; however, I note that in February 1934, we im-

I am sorry I could not follow in detail what the hon. member (Mr. Girouard) said with regard to imports and exports of butter and cheese. In that year we exported 233,980,716 pounds. In the year ending March, 1908 that had decreased to 189,710,463. Coming down to more recent years, in the year ending March, 1926, our exports of cheese were 148,333,500 pounds, and in the year ending March, 1927, they had dropped to 136,665,400; in the year ending March, 1928, they were 105,212,600; in 1929-30 they were 92,293,700, and in 193031 they were down to 79,590,400-that is, in March, at the end of that fiscal year. In other words, from the year ending March, 1926, to the end of the fiscal year in which the government changed, the reduction in exports was some 47 per cent, from 148,0100,000 pounds to 79,000,000 pounds. In the year ending March, 1932, the exports of cheese had increased to 85,424,700, or about 8 per cent, and in the year ended March 31, 1933, the last year for which we have information, the exports were 85,711,600 pounds.
With regard to the imports of cheese in the corresponding years, in the year ending March, 1926, the imports into Canada were 6,678,757 pounds, and during the year ending March, 1933, the imports of cheese into Canada had dropped to 1,103,391 pounds. This cheese is practically all of a type that is not made in Canada.
Now for the imports and exports of butter. In 1926-27 the imports of butter were 7,029,084; in 1927-28 they were 15,626,007; in 1928-29 they had increased to 25,609 915; and in 1929-30 the figure was 41,919,372. The hon. member quoted the imports of butter for 1931, but that is really for nine months of the year 1930, because the 1931 figure is from March 31, 1930, to March 31, 1931, when we imported 16,500,801 pounds. In 1931-32 the imports were down to 879,670 pounds and in 1932-33 they were 876,894 pounds. This shows that butter from outside the dominion has not been coming in during the past two years to any very considerable extent to interfere with the market for butter in Canada.
'Mr. BEAUBIEN: Can the minister gave any reasons why our exports of cheese have diminished to the extent they have, and why to-day we occupy fourth position instead of first? What is the cause?

New Zealand is the only country that stands ahead of Canada in exports of cheese to the United Kingdom. If we had produced more cheese there would no doubt have been more cheese exported, but the reason we have not produced more, in addition to what I have given, I would say is that the market for the greater part of our cheese is the United Kingdom, therefore the price is the world price, and the world price of cheese has been forced down during the past two or three years particularly. When the farmer has the choice of taking, say, nine to eleven cents per pound for his cheese or getting a fair price for his milk converted into butter, the tendency is for the milk or cream to be diverted to the creameries for the manufacture of butter. That has led to a decrease in our production of cheese, which of course leads to the decrease in our exports.

Did the minister say
11 cents a pound for cheese?
I took that as an example.
Does the minister suggest that taking 17i to 181 cents for butter rather than 11 cents for cheese is sound business?

To produce an equal return the price of cheese should be 50 per cent of the price of butter or butter fat. But a farmer ha's to take other considerations into account, not only the price he will get for his cheese in comparison with butter, but in connection with butter the value of the by-product, the skim milk for the feeding of pigs and other uses on the farm.

I happen to know a little about cheese. When I was a boy we used to take milk to the cheese factory, and I found that you could make more money by sending it there with cheese at say 9 cents a pound than by turning it into butter at 20 cents, even taking into consideration the by-products. And the farmer who takes his milk to a cheese factory has by-products, though they are probably not of as much value as if he separated his milk and shipped the cream.
It seems to me that there is confusion about these statistics, whether intentional or not I do not know. The minister says that according to his information we occupy second place in the market of Great Britain in regard to cheese exports. When I said a
[Mr. Beaubien.l
moment ago that we had fallen from first to fourth place in regard to all countries I made a mistake, this bulletin says:
Relative position of suppliers or exporters of cheese to Great Britain.
That is for January, 1934; it distinctly says that we occupied fourth position. If the minister's information is correct, that we occupy second place, while these bulletins that are circulated to the members almost every day show that we occupy fourth position, there is something wrong. It is confusing. The other day the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) complained about discrepancies in the statistics, and the same thing is very clearly brought out here.
If I heard the hon. member correctly, the bulletin which he quotes states that the position of Canada as exporter of cheese to the world market-
No, I said that at first, but I corrected it-to the British market.
-was fourth. For what period is that? Is it just for the month of January?

This bulletin, dated
March 9, 1934, says:
The relative position of Canada among the exporters of cheese to Great Britain in January, 1934. . . .
There is no contradiction in the two statements. My statement was based on the yearly exports. In Canada very little cheese is made in the winter in comparison with the summer months.
This bulletin says January, 1934. I suppose the comparison is with January, 1933, or why should they mention January specially?
It is a monthly bulletin: that would be the relative position during the month of January.

So you can take January as a basis. You could take March or any month so far as that is concerned, but you compare a month of 1934 with the same month of 1933, I suppose. Taking the government's own bulletin, our position as exporter of cheese to Great Britain in January, 1934, compared to January, 1933, was fourth place.

In the winter months our production of cheese is much less, therefore we would stand in a lower position in regard to exports. In view of cheese being so much more of a summer product, the only fair

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
comparison is on the yearly basis. The point 1 was making is that the statement there that we were fourth in our exports to the United Kingdom for January is not contradictory in any way to the statement I made as to the yearly exports.

Does the minister contend, then, that our exports of cheese in January were small because that is an off season? Does the minister contend that cheese is exported the month it is made? My understanding has been different.

A great deal of our cheese is exported when it is very green, to a much greater extent than was the case a number of years ago. We feel that this is one of the criticisms we have to make with regard to the cheese industry at the present time. If it were possible to hold the cheese longer and cure it more it perhaps would go on the old country market in better condition, but today cheese is exported to a very great extent when it is green, and the people who purchase it in the United Kingdom cure it there.

How long after a cheese is made is it fit for the export market?
Mr, WEIR (Melfort): It depends on the export market, and the same applies to the domestic market. Some people will buy cheese when it is green and when other people might consider not cured at all. An average statement is unsatisfactory, but a great deal of our cheese is exported within one to three months after it is made, depending on the locality and on conditions in the locality.
Then with regard to the month of January, the basis of production has nothing to do with the low export at all, if the cheese is exported when it is about three months old. Is that right?
One to three months.

Has the Department of Agriculture any way of ascertaining whether the cheese is properly matured before it is exported? If we are going to keep on in the dairying industry, as I think we will have to because of the prices paid for cereals, has the department any way of inspecting this cheese in order to see that it is in proper condition before it leaves our shores, so that we may be able to hold the market we have to-day and perhaps, in time, regain part of the market we have lost? As the minister knows, dairying is a very hard industry to carry on; it entails a great deal of work and a man is r"allv tied down to the farm.

With reference to the time of export amy information is that mutch cheese is exported within one to three months after it is manufactured. There is another element that enters here and that would apply particularly in our winter months; Quebec and Ontario, and particularly eastern Ontario, which are the large cheese producing districts in Canada, rush off all the cheese possible before navigation in the St. Lawrence closes, because of freight rates.
All cheese for export is graded. As a result of criticisms received from the United Kingdom to the effect that some of our cheese arrived there not in the best possible condition because it was shipped too green, we have taken steps to stamp the date on the cheese itself. That action has been taken by regulation. We have no power, however, to interfere with the export of the cheese at any time beyond grading it and having it dated so that those who get it will know how long it has been since the cheese was manufactured.

With reference to the statement made by the minister a few moments ago as to our position in regard to cheese exports I should like to refer to a paragraph in the commercial bulletin which states that during 1033 New Zealand reaffirmed its position on the export market, when she exported 8,743 tons of a total importation by Great Britain of 9,097 tons. Australia exported 217 tons, Ireland 91 tons, and Canada 46 tons.

What period are
those figures for?

According to the bulletin they are for the entire year of 1933. The paragraph states that New Zealand reaffirmed its position and in fact, as I interpret it, may gain on the export market. New Zealand and Australia certainly have trimmed us to a frazzle in the export of cheese. I am sorry the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) is not ihere; I remember tlhat he and many other hon. gentlemen now sitting opposite shed crocodile tears because of what the King government did to the dairying industry. In fact I remember how the genial Minister of Railways stated, in and out of this house, how the King government was ruining the agricultural industry, how they were reducing the chances of the farmers to make a living on the land. I never saw such a sympathetic bunch in my life as they were during the session of 1930. They had a bureau in a building across Wellington street, with a staff of I do not know how many-

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
Am hon. MEMBER:	It worked fine.

It certainly did, but it
will not work again. To-day the standing of those people who tried to fool the farmers in those days-I am speaking politically-is not very high. The farmers know they were fooled; that is shown by the figures in these bulletins, and the minister cannot deny it. The farmers have been deceived by this government; they have been induced and in fact almost forced by circumstances to go into the dairying industry. The minister knows that when cereal prices are low and a farmer cannot get enough from the sale of cereals to buy the necessities of life he has to go into the dairying industry even if he only receives a small amount, because he needs ready cash. The minister knows that today no farmer can go to a bank and get a penny, and the minister also knows that a farmer must have some cows in order to get a few pennies together with which to buy tea and sugar, even with a two cent excise tax on sugar. There must be some reason for New Zealand and Australia taking the place of Canada in the export of cheese. If one compared the present price of butter with the price of cheese I think he would find that it would be more profitable to take milk to the cheese factory. Either we are not producing enough cheese, we are not producing the quality of cheese, or there is something wrong with our commercial intelligence or trade agencies in Great Britain. I think that these statistics and the information contained in the commercial bulletin of the government certainly need some explanation. I hope the minister will be able to justify the figures and will be able to give us good and sufficient reasons why we are occupying that position to-day. Especially should he do so in view of the fact that the minister must take the responsibility for the Conservative party in regard to the propaganda which during the last election campaign they spread throughout the country. They promised a higher price for butter, they promised a higher price for cheese, they promised the Mafeking cutoff,-they promised everything. These are the results of the promises made by this government and the candidates representing it in 1030.

With reference to
the statements of the hon. member to the effect that this government misled the farmers, may I say that no one person can speak for every speech made throughout all parts of the country. So far as my own information goes, however, I say that the promise of this party was that we would endeavour, first of all, to give the Canadian market to Canadian farmers, and I maintain that we have carried

out that promise. The effect of our action, translated into dollars and cents-a process which is more understandable to the farmer than would be a theoretical statement about markets-is this: The right hon. leader of the party, to which the hon. member who has just spoken gives his allegiance, has made the statement that if he were returned to power the duties would be placed where they were when he left office.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member
says "hear, hear." In dollars and cents the right hon. gentleman's statement means only this: Had the policies advocated by him been in force in April, 1933, the export value of our butter at that date would have been 10-94 cents per pound. I have figures here for other months, but I do not wish to bore the committee with them.

Is the figure given by
the minister one which he suggests would have obtained had the present right hon. leader of the opposition been in power?

Yes, if our tariff
had been put where the right hon. gentleman said he would put it, namely, at the same place it was when he and his party left office. Had that been in effect the value of butter in Montreal would have been 10-94 cents per pound, plus the import duty of one cent.

This must be a dream
the minister is having. Can he substantiate what he is saying or the figures he is giving?

Yes, my figures are absolutely correct,. This is based on the export market in London. In the same week the premium on our butter, brought about by the action this government did take, and said during the election campaign it would take- not that the price of butter would be raised but that the market would be given to the Canadian farmer-was 18-06 cents per pound higher. That is, the premium over the export market was 18-06 cents per pound, which is an increase of more than 150 per cent over the price which the farmer would have got for his butter had he been selling it, at that particular time, under the arrangement promised by the right hon. gentleman opposite in the event of his being returned to power.
Oh, oh.
That is a dream.
AVhat would have been the price of butter had the C.C.F. been in power?

Would the minister tell us the duty?

Supply

Agriculture-Dairying
Mr. WEIR Melfort):	There is nothing
which would give me greater pleasure than to answer all questions at once, but I think the discussion would be of greater value and of more interest to hon. members, and I would be in a better .position to give information, if I were allowed to answer one question at a time. With the exception of the months of September and part of the month of October, in the year 1933, a premium existed over the export market during the months of January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, November and December.
Will the minister tell us the duty on New Zealand butter?
I should like to answer the question asked by one hon. member before answering that of another.
I will have a whole lot more to ask.

That is fine; we welcome the questions. The bulletin to which reference was made appears to contain the information that for the year 1933 Canada was in fourth place, so far as the importation of cheese into the United Kingdom was concerned. I have before me the monthly report of the United Kingdom showing the figures on imports of cheese. The report indicates that in 1933 Canada exported 70,528,080 pounds, New Zealand, 230,652,016 pounds and Australia-and I understood the hon. member to say that Australia had a greater export to the United Kingdom than had Canada-is given the figure of 10,357,000. I do not think there will be very much gained by discussing across the floor of the committee any comparison of statistics the hon. member has in front of him and those I have in front of me unless I am given a copy of his figures and have an opportunity to study them.
I shall be very pleased to give the minister a copy when I am through with them.

In 1900 the total production of butter in Canada was 30,066,739 pounds; in 1932 the total production of creamery butter was 214,002,127 pounds. At the same time the production of cheese decreased from 220,833.269 pounds in 1900 to 120,524,243 pounds in 1932.
That is not so, according to the information the minister gave a little while ago.
We have three sets of figures now.
One set gives exports, and the other production. In 1929 the production of cheese was 118,746,286 pounds; less than it was in 1932. In 1930, the production was 119,105,203 pounds.

Mr. Chairman, I must
say I have had dreams similar to the one the minister has been describing to the house when I have dreamed of a comparison between what the farmers would have received had the right hon. leader of the opposition been in power and what they have received since this government has had office. But I must give to the minister and to the committee my reasons for such dreams: I had been out the night before. Let us compare the price of butter between the years 1926 and 1930 with-
Oh, oh.

The hon. member for
Compton laughs; why is he not fair? Why is not the minister fair in his comparisons?

Compare with the world
prices.

The minister knows he cannot substantiate what he has just said as to prices the farmer would have received had the right hon. leader of the opposition been in power. He knows that better than anybody.
London is where we sell our butter.

Will you kindly keep
quiet? You have said two or three words too many in this house for your own good. The less you say from now on the better for you.
That is your point of view.

The minister has not
yet explained to me, and I should like his explanation before this item passes, why Australia and New Zealand occupy the position they do to-day, and not only that but have strengthened their position in the market of Great Britain while Canada has not done so. I will send a copy of this bulletin over to the minister so that he may see the figures for himself. If they are not correct, why are they published?
Might I ask the hon. member to read from the bulletin the Australian exports to the United Kingdom market for the year to which he refers.
During 1933?

Read it.

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying '

I am going to read it,
but it is in French, and I will translate it as I go along, and the translation will be just as good as the translating that will be done under the Secretary of State's new bureau.
Read it in Irish. To-morrow is St. Patrick's day.

He would sure be right
then.

Here are the exact words:
During 1933 New Zealand reaffirmed its position on the markets when its exportation amounted to 8,743 tons.
To the United Kingdom market?

Yes. It goes on:
Out of a total importation of 9,098 tons Australia contributed 217 tons, Canada 46 tons and the Irish Free State 91 tons.
Forty-six tons for Canada?
Yes.
And Australia two hundred odd?

That is what it says. I will read it again:
During 1933-
Is that for the entire year?

It says, "During 1933." That must mean the whole year:
During 1933 New' Zealand reaffirmed its position on the markets when its exportation amounted to 8.743 tons. Out of a total importation of 9.098 tons, Australia contributed 217 tons, Canada 46 tons and the Irish Free State 91 tons.
Even the Irish beat us.
That is for one year?

He has given you what it
says.

The hon. member at the outset said something about having dreams, and that what I said was not based on fact. What I stated was based first of all on the statement of the right hon. leader of the opposition that if he was returned to power the duty would be lowered or placed where it was when he went out of power. But we do not need to go back. At the present time the price of butter in Montreal is 29? to 30 cents a pound wholesale. The price of the finest Australian butter in London is 15-7 cents per pound. Now if the duty imposed against importations of butter into

this country was one cent a pound, which was the duty at the time the present opposition went out of power, Australia could pay that cent a pound duty and deliver their butter here at 16-7 cents a pound, which would mean a difference from- the present price of 12 or 13 cents a pound.

May I ask the minister a question right at that point? In view of the figures given by the hon. member for Drumm ond-A r tibab a ska (Mr. Girouard) a little while ago of the importations of butter from Australia and New Zealand, will the minister tell the committee how much more the Canadian farmer would be receiving for his butter to-day if this government had prevented the importation of that Australian and New Zealand butter? It is just as logical for me to ask that question as for the minister to make the comparison he does.
The butter imported into Canada during each of the past two years, as I read earlier, was less than one million pounds.
But suppose it had not been imported, what would have been the difference in the price?

If it had not been imported the price certainly would not have been lower. Therefore the figures that I quote are at least safe figures. If that butter had not come in we might naturally expect that there might have been some increase in price, but the amount imported was only two-days' supply of butter for the whole dominion. This butter has been let in up to the quantity that I have stated, and in spite of that our butter is at the price it is, but if it were not for the present duty butter would be coming into this country to-day on the same basis as it enters the United Kingdom at the price stated, plus the duty.

In other words, that means that the importations of butter under the Liberal regime decreased the price of butter to the Canadian farmer, while importations of butter under the Conservative regime increased the price of butter to the Canadian farmer. That is the only conclusion one can draw.
You let in 35,000,000 pounds under the Liberal government, at a cent a pound duty.

The reason why we imported butter from 1926 to 1930, and no one knows it better than my hon. friend is that we wanted our people to have butter on their bread-that and no other reason.

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
You let it come in here because you had no weapon to keep it out. Everybody knows that, and that is why the farmers voted against it.
Nobody knows better than my hon. friend that any time cereals reach the prices prevailing from 1926 to 1930 the farmers are not going to produce dairy products unless they are crazy.
Speak for your farmers.
I am speaking for our farmers. You have no farmers in your part of the country.
I have better farmers than you ever dared to be.

The minister knows well that when the farmer can get 60 and 65 cents for his barley, 50 and 60 cents for oats, and $1.25 for wheat, he is not going to milk cows unless he has to. If you compare the prices received for butter in 1926 with those received in 1930 you will find that they were higher then than under this regime.
Ten cents a pound.

And that in spite of no
duty. The minister seeks to interject a political side to this issue when I am quite serious in my efforts to help the farmers. He stated that if the Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King had been Prime Minister such and such a thing would have happened while such and such a thing has happened because he and his colleagues are in power. I think he is going beyond the facts and is giving us just a little dream of his own. The minister has not answered my question as to why Australia increased her importations of cheese into the British market while Canada's imports continued to go down. I should like to know why this has happened in the face of the promises made and the glowing pictures painted during the last elections. I want to get this point clear as it is something the farmers want to know.

With reference to
the matter of political interjection and the hon. member being so serious for the welfare of the farmer, the committee might note that he started his own statement with the words "speaking from a political standpoint."

That was an answer I
gave to some back-bencher who interrupted me.

What are you, a front
bencher?

The hon. member
quoted from the Commercial Intelligence Journal and sought to show that Canada had taken fourth place in the exports of cheese to the United Kingdom. I shall read from this bulletin for the information of the committee.
Is that the French copy?
No.

I was reading from the
French copy.

The statement
which the hon. member read is headed "butter" not "cheese." This reads:
New Zealand imports of butter into Avon-mouth have again moved upward. In 1932 they amounted to 5,908 tons out of a total import of 6,200 tons, and those from Australia amounted to 226 tons compared with 29 tons from Canadian ports.

The hon. minister will
notice the portion marked from which the hon. member quoted.

I was starting at
the beginning.
Do not mix it up with the cheese.
They do not mix.

It is all under the
same heading of "butter." It continues:
During 1933 New Zealand strengthened her hold on the market by increasing to 8,743 tons out of a total import of 9,098 tons, Australia contributing 217 tons, Canada 46 tons, and the Irish Free State 91 tons. Danish and Russian butter is sold in quantity but supplies are not imported direct.
Mr. VALLANCE. Would the minister mind sending that over.

If the minister mixes
butter and cheese it will be a new mixture.

I was not mixing
them.

There is a good reason why
New Zealand and Australia have captured a large share of the market in Great Britain. For the last three years the British pound has been worth a considerable premium in Australia and New Zealand. About a year and a half ago the British pound was worth fifty per cent more to the Australian exporter in his own currency than it was to the Canadian. This is the real reason why Australia and New Zealand have taken the butter and cheese market from the Canadian producer.

Criminal Code-Race Meetings

This all goes to prove
that we should have a new translation system. The minister gave me the exports of cheese to Great Britain in 1933, and I should like to have them for 1932.

The exports of
cheese for the year ended March 31, 1933, amounted to 85,711,600 pounds; for 1932, 85,424,700 pounds, which is less and for 1931, 79,590,400 pounds, still less.

Following up the remarks of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), the other night when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) was trying to get some estimates through it was pointed out that we were not holding the trade in wheat and cereals between Great Britain and Canada. I think the whole thing resolves itself into the difference in exchange. Because of the sound money policy of this government we now find ourselves in this position. The minister compared the position of the farmers of Canada between 1926 and 1930 with their position in later years and tried to make out that that position had been improved. He knows just as well as I that that argument cannot stand and will not be accepted by the farmers.

I was answering a
statement made by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien).

The farmer of western
Canada and of eastern Canada as well has never been in the plight in which he finds himself to-day. I do not wish to go over the promises made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and members of his party during the throes of the last general elections, but in February, 1932, the price of wheat was the lowest it had been in four hundred years. In *the face of this fact we have the minister standing up and trying to convince this committee that to-day the farmer is in a more enviable position in connection with butter production than he was from 1926 to 1930.
I did not state that.

Sour
grapes; you do not want to see the price of butter go up.
Progress reported.
