subtopic: RACE MEETINGS OF FOURTEEN CONSECUTIVE DAYS INSTEAD OF TWO SEVEN DAY PERIODS

speechtext: Hon. RAYMOND D. MORAND (East Essex) moved the second reading of Bill No. 35, to amend the criminal code (race meetings).

subtopic: RACE MEETINGS OF FOURTEEN CONSECUTIVE DAYS INSTEAD OF TWO SEVEN DAY PERIODS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: RACE MEETINGS OF FOURTEEN CONSECUTIVE DAYS INSTEAD OF TWO SEVEN DAY PERIODS
speechtext: The purpose of the bill is simply to remove the present twenty day period that intervenes between two race meetings of seven days each: it has nothing to do with the principle of racing or with increasing the number of days of racing. Under the criminal code as it stands, a period of twenty days must elapse between one race meeting of seven days and the next meeting of seven days. With conditions as they are now, particularly in our city, in view of the fact that the state of Michigan now has racing one hundred and twenty days in the year, it is difficult for those having investments in race tracks in our city to find ways and means of holding two meetings of seven days each, whereas it would be easier to have a meeting of fourteen consecutive days.

subtopic: RACE MEETINGS OF FOURTEEN CONSECUTIVE DAYS INSTEAD OF TWO SEVEN DAY PERIODS
speechtext: This does not increase the total number of days?

subtopic: RACE MEETINGS OF FOURTEEN CONSECUTIVE DAYS INSTEAD OF TWO SEVEN DAY PERIODS
speechtext: No, nor the total number of races.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: RACE MEETINGS OF FOURTEEN CONSECUTIVE DAYS INSTEAD OF TWO SEVEN DAY PERIODS
speechtext:
I have no objection to the bill being read the second time, but I would ask that it do not go into committee until we have had an opportunity of communicating with the various provincial governments on the subject. They are entitled to a certain amount of taxation on the pari mutue.1 system, and I should like to ascertain whether they have any objection to the proposed change.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Morand in the chair.
Dairying, $234,000.

Before the house rose at six o'clock we had discussed this item for about an hour, and it was also under consideration on another occasion. I do not wish

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
to prolong the debate to any extent, but there are a number of things that might be discussed here, particularly some of the statements made this afternoon. Those of us who were here in
1925	will recall that butter became a political issue after the enactment of the Australian treaty in 1925-I think it was then. From that day to this it has been more or less a political issue.
Now, while I do not think that we should spend too much time going over ancient history, nevertheless, in order to make the record right, I wish to make a few references to that occasion. The price of butter in 1925 was high, running between 35 and 40 cents per pound wholesale, basis No. 1 pasteurized in the city of Montreal on January 1. At the election of 1925 and also at the election of
1926	it was attempted by the then leader of the Conservative party, now leader of the Senate, to make more or less of a political issue of this subject; but butter being so high, it was difficult to do that and it did not cut very much ice, if at all, in either election. In 1930, however, the same treaty was still in vogue, although there was in it one anticipated change introduced by the Hon. Mr. Dunning in his last budget on May day 1930, in which he intimated to the house that he had given notice to the Australian government, and I 'believe to the government of New Zealand as well, that after October the duty on butter from the antipodes would revert to 4 cents-what it had been for the previous quarter of a century. I would point out that it was really 4 cents, and had the Liberals come into power it would have been 4 cents. The minister's calculation is wrong when it is suggested that it would have been only one cent had the Liberals come into power again in 1930.
We come now to the present day, and before going any further I would direct the attention of the house to the fact that while the Australian treaty was the occasion of a political issue, for four successive years after the enactment of that treaty, butter averaged 40 cents per pound in Montreal on January 1, basis No. 1 pasteurized. It can readily be appreciated therefore that in view of that high price not much of an issue could be made of butter, notwithstanding the fact that the duty had been reduced to one cent a pound; and one of the reasons why we reduced it to one cent per pound was simply that this was in accordance with the general policy of making treaties with any empire or other government on the basis of lower and not of higher tariffs. That might have been a political
mistake but it was not an economic mistake; it was not a mistake so far as the interests of the consumers were concerned, and when the high price to the producers was what it was then. Why, farmers would think they were in clover to-day if butter in Montreal were 40 cents a pound. Last fall it was less than half that amount. During 1929 and particularly during 1930, butter, naturally with other commodities, went down and it was then that the terrific onslaught was made on the Australian treaty, with appreciable results, in the province of Quebec at all events. Probably [DOT]most of the seats lost to the Liberal party in that province were attributed to the Australian treaty; the treaty was blamed for it. *There are a number of other reasons I will not discuss; it is past history. The question [DOT]is, what are we to do now? What are the causes of present butter prices?
Last fall, I remember, some of us were in [DOT]Mackenzie riding doing some big game hunting, and butter fat in the month of October [DOT]was exactly 14 cents per pound, just half [DOT]what it is to-day. I have word from my [DOT]home to-day that the last can of cream we sold fetched 28 cents, on the basis of butter fat for table cream, twice what it was last October. You cannot credit that to the byelection in Mackenzie; there are a number of causes to which it can be attributed. One cause however is that butter is scarcer now, and no doubt scarcer all over the world. I do not know what stocks there are throughout the world or in cold storage here, but this condition cannot be attributed either to the by-election in Mackenzie or to the Ottawa pacts because that was a year and a half ago, and the downward tendency persisted after that. It cannot be attributed to the present duty on Australian butter because that was on last fall also. We shall have therefore to leave it to the minister to explain why the price was only 14 cents last fall whereas to-day it is exactly twice as much. It is difficult to find reasons for this, because we can argue about anything from statistics. You know what is said about statistics-of course I will not repeat it here, but there is more or less truth in it. We are statistically cured now. We are getting such a dose of them we may be spoiled if we get overdosed.
But I am concerned about another matter. I find that according to a bulletin I have here, issued jointly by the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce, there is some danger of our being asked to restrict still further our exports to the old country. The hon. member for

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) referred this afternoon to the reduction in exports of cheese. The reports indicate that almost every month these export British quotas are going on for various Canadian commodities; first on wheat, then on cattle, oats and eggs, and now we are told there is going to be a quota on dairy products from the antipodes, and very likely we may be asked to apply it to dairy products from Canada. Before going any further I would like the minister to give us some assurance regarding quotas on our dairy products. These gentleman's agreements with the motherland are very nice, but there is an Empire bargain, and while there was not much in it at any time for us in the matter of dairy products there will be still less if a quota is put on our cheese, still further restricting our exports. I would like to know what the situation is, if there is anything pending as far as the minister knows as to a quota being put on dairy products from Canada, or from the antipodes either, by Great Britain.

Answering the last
question first, as far as my information goes there is nothing to lead us to believe at present that a quota would be put on against our dairy products. I believe that matter has been under discussion between the Australian and the New Zealand and the United Kingdom officials.
Going back to the statement made by the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Val-lance) before the committee rose, I do not think anyone could justly give the interpretation he did to anything I said as to the comparative condition of farmers in Canada in 1929 or 1930 and the present time.
There is no comparison.

I realize that the
condition of agriculture in Canada is not what we would like in many respects. The condition of farmers in practically all countries has become very much worse since the beginning of what is called the great depression. The only comparison that could fairly be made would be between normal conditions in various countries and the conditions as they exist at the present time.
With reference to the price of butter fat being 14 cents a pound in the fall and 28 cents at the present time, when butter fat was at 14 cents we had accumulated in Canada a stock of butter greater than was required for our own consumption. The butter in storage in September was about 42,000,000 pounds, which I believe proved a

surprise to most of the trade, and when they realized, upon the report coming out, that storage stocks had reached that amount they became alarmed, seeing that the price they had been paying averaged some four cents per pound more than would have been warranted had they realized that we were going on an export basis. That forced them to export some butter, and therefore the price fell to that of the export market. At that time we called a conference and were able to have some of the different holders of butter-and some who were not holders, as they felt it would be healthy for the trade -export some butter from Canada even at a loss. Therefore the reason for the price of butter being what it was then was that we were forced on the world market. At the present time we are very near a balance of production and consumption. That is why the market is what it is at present.
Mr. MOTHERWEI/L: I think that explanation is quite logical. Canada was aiming not to be obliged to export any butter, just to meet our own requirements, so that we might artificially, by means of a tariff get more than the export price. Whether that is an attainable and ambitious object I leave to the committee to decide. Since then some export has taken place, relieving the pressure on the market, and prices have responded.
My hon. friend indicated that he did not think there was any danger of a quota being imposed on our butter, although there had been some discussion with regard to the antipodes. That is all the information that I have as to the antipodes. But we have here a bulletin called "The Agricultural Situation," and, a significant thing, it is put out by two ministers, so it ought to be doubly right. There are not going to be any mistakes about this bulletin; two ministers will stand behind its accuracy. It states that it is-
Published' by authority of the Hon. R. Weir, Minister of Agriculture, and the Hon. H. H. Stevens, Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I wonder if this is significant in connection with what we hear every day, that these two departments are going to merge, with the Department of Trade and Commerce on the outside. The minister perhaps can give me some particulars about that also. Anyway this is a nicely gotten up bulletin. Here is what it says about the dairy products quota question, on page 28:
The large and increasing volume of butter and cheese imported into the United Kingdom has caused the British government to enter into discussions with New Zealand and

Australia with a view to the voluntary restriction of exports of these products to the United Kingdom. If any such agreements are concluded between the United Kingdom and New Zealand and Australia, Canada may be asked to take similar action;
That brings up the whole question of how far Canada is to go to meet Great Britain in the matter of these quotas, and how long it is going to take for us to be squeezed out of the British market with a lot of our farm commodities. That is what we are heading for, as far as I can see. On the next page it says:
The possibility of restrictions on imports of dairy products into the United Kingdom would suggest that it would be advisable for Canadian producers to develop home consumption as much as possible.
I hope that advice will not be given to us in regard to wheat, that we will have to eat all we produce, because that is more than we can do, and feel comfortable. But our butter quality has improved and has been improving for years. Our consumption per capita I think is the highest in the world, and the home market in Canada is a great factor, because even this year we have been coming pretty close to eating all we produce. But if that is to be our aim in all farm products we will be known as a tail-end country, just dragging along. Canada has been known as a great agricultural country, better known for that than possibly anything else; are we to aim to supply only our own requirements in such products as butter, bacon and eggs and other such farm products.
Reverting to this bulletin, I am afraid there is more in this merger proposition than may appear. I can recall that at one time copyrights and patents which now come under the Trade and Commerce, were under the Department of Agriculture. Grain never was under the Department of Agriculture; in the last century it was under the Department of Inland Revenue, among the tobaccos and whiskies, and from there is was transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce. In the past these various services have been in the habit of gravitating from agriculture to trade and commerce to help make that a better and more important department, and I am afraid if the minister is not on his guard they will be swiping something more from agriculture when he is not looking. He had a very excellent official representing the Department of Agriculture in London when this government came into power, but it was not long before the Minister of Trade and Commerce had that most capable gentleman in his own department, bag, boots and body, and I know he got hold of a good man.
Now we have this joint bulletin which I hold in my hand. Is this another step in the direction of absorption of Agriculture by Trade and Commerce? I want to tell the minister that if anything like that is going on he can depend upon at least one individual to back him up in resisting it; I will do all I can in that way. As a matter of fact, if there is to be any swiping or changing it should be in the direction of having agriculture all under one minister, and logically that should be the Minister of Agriculture. I know of no country in the world that has agriculture under two ministers; it only results in more confusion and more mistakes, and I question if either department will be any better off by this sort of interlocking of departments. It is all right to have a companionate marriage which can be dissolved as quickly as possible after disillusionment, but I should not like this merger proposal to go any further. The farmers do not want to be running after two ministers. In connection with the proposed marketing act the general report on the street is that it will be under the Department of Trade and Commerce. Our farmers want to go to the Minister of Agriculture when they want anything; they do not want to be trotting after two ministers, and I repeat the logical, proper and sympathetic place for them to go is to the Minister of Agriculture. I think perhaps if the minister would give us some assurance on that point we would not need to talk any more about this matter. A word from him would be sufficient, and I hope he does not mind the candour with which I have discussed the question. Those are the facts, and we have the evidence here in this merger bulletin.

In the first place
my information is that the per capita consumption of butter in Canada is 30| pounds, while in New Zealand and Australia it is 35 pounds. If our consumption were to increase to that extent we would wipe out the exports of all dairy products.
With reference to the bulletin, it is the outcome to a large extent of a series of conferences between the various provincial departments of agriculture, those connected with agricultural colleges and with provincial and federal institutions, which culminated in a conference in Toronto in 1932 at which it was agreed that by getting together and discussing the problems of agriculture and the possible means of solving those difficulties a good deal of duplication and wastage would be eliminated. It was felt that in publications alone there was a great deal of wastage and duplica-

tion, and sometimes' disagreement, so it was decided to set up a committee representative of these organizations interested in agriculture. The committee named was composed of one member from the federal department, Doctor Booth; Doctor Grindley of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and Professor Lattimer of Macdonald College. Their first publication, I believe, was the Agricultural Situation, which I think hon. gentlemen interested in agriculture will agree was a commendable contribution for a beginning, and which served the purpose of assembling the combined thought of the various interested organizations. It is quite apparent that the minister is not greatly enamoured of this proposed absorption at all events; I am glad he is not, and I need not discuss it further.
Now I wonder if I dare refer to a matter which has been rather controversial on this side of the house, as well as on the ministerial side. It seems to me that dairying is too closely associated with the national life and national health of Canada to be discriminated against as is the case at present. I am referring to the grant which formerly was made to the National Dairy Council. Two or three members on this side of the house took some objection to the activities of the council prior to the last election; I always said that even if they were indiscreet they were not half as much so as the gentlemen who composed the horticultural council. I do not think either organization should be tied down in connection with public questions; that is my own personal view. That is the ground I have taken, though possibly other hon. gentlemen will differ with me on that point. I do not think they will differ, however, as to the principle that either these grants should remain in all these branches of agriculture or they should be eliminated from all branches. I think that is a fair proposition. I am not suggesting that they should be eliminated in any branch, but I realize how much dairying means not only to the east but also to the west where it is becoming more important all the time, and it does seem too bad that this one branch of agriculture, founded on that old standby the dairy cow, which never fails no matter how much prices may vary, should be discriminated against. The old cow keeps on freshening and producing her milk from which come the many dairy products into which milk is processed. They go on year after year, no matter what happens; they never fail. Yet there is

no government grant for her. When I turn to the estimates of two or three years ago I find a grant of $5,000 for the National Dairy Council. I was not responsible for it; I do not feel sensitive about that grant disappearing because I did not initiate it. It was done before my time, though it is true that on my recommendation the grant was increased. Does not the hon. gentleman think that the National Dairy Council, which is composed of excellent men, has been disciplined enough and without cause through the elimination of the grant for two years? Does he not think the grant should be restored so that all these organizations will be on a parity? Is that not a fair proposal? I am sure the minister would feel inclined that way. I do not think there would be much fuss over here if that were done, and even if there were the minister only has to look at the noses he can count over there in his rear guard. You can do what you like in any case, but if this grant is restored I shall not be tempted to make an issue of the matter in the next election. There are enough public issues without bothering with this matter important as it is. I should like to see this discrimination remedied if possible.

In dealing with the
Canadian quota into the British market, the hon. member for Melfort suggested a question to my mind which I should like to direct to the minister. I should like him to correct me if I am wrong. Is the importation of Canadian cattle into the British market the same for the first three months of this year as it was last year?
It is more this year.
That is, it is extended now to six months, do I understand?
Yes.
Has the minister any reason to give us as to why the British government has seen fit to take this action?

The action was taken because of a number of circumstances. In the first place, when it was forecast that a very severe embargo was to be imposed against Irish cattle going into the United Kingdom, old country buyers before the imposition of this regulation bought all the cattle from Ireland, that they had money to buy with, or that they could borrow with which to buy, I believe. The result was that they had more cattle on hand than they had feed with which to properly look after them. Some of those cattle in the spring of 1933 were being forced on the market in a more or less unfinished condition and in quantities which had a depressing effect upon the market. Then, to accentuate that condition, in July and August of last year, a drought which had been unprecedented for years in the old land reduced pasturage to the point where they were forced to put on the market still more cattle than those people who were in the best position to forecast had thought possible. These cattle, too, were not finished as well as they should have been. Because of this drought, the root crop in the old country was very much below normal. Those hon. members who are acquainted with methods of feeding obtaining in the old country will understand that the basic food is supplied by the root crop. Especially is that so, I believe, in Scotland. This shortage continued the process of forcing cattle on the market in an unfinished condition, and in greater quantities. The Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries in the old land, hoping to improve the price of cattle, followed the same line he had followed with reference to bacon, and placed an embargo of fifty per cent against the importation of Irish cattle. That is, they could export to the United Kingdom only fifty per cent of the cattle they had exported during the same period ir

previous years. The Irish Free State, not to be outdone, and to show that they did not have to do what the United Kingdom said they should do, decided they would take matters in their own hands and would not export as many cattle, even, as Great Britain had stipulated they would be allowed. That is the rather incongruous position now obtaining. At the same time the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries asked that we cooperate with them to hold off the market as many cattle as possible to see if the price would not go up. At first they asked that for three months we would not ship any more. They did not ask for a cut in our shipments, but simply that we would not ship any more in the first three months of 1934 than we had in the first three of 1933. That was felt to be not entirely satisfactory, because our first shipment in 1933 did not begin, to any extent, until late in January, and after negotiations had taken place the period was extended to six months. We feel that there is a probability-and I would not like to put it any stronger than that-that with any improvement of conditions, before the expiration of six months, if we can show it will be a hardship on us, there may be a further extension.

Following up the reasons given by the minister, may I offer some others which were produced on the floor of the British House of Commons. So it appears that we are not going to be permitted to ship any more cattle from the first of January, 1934, to the end of June, 1934, than we did during the corresponding period in 1933. But the quota in 1933 was applicable only to the first three months. I should like to ask the minister this question: Does this new order of the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries in the British House of Commons apply also to oats and eggs?
{Mr. R. Weir.]

My understanding
is that it does not apply to eggs. I am not in a position to say whether or not it applies to oats. My own impression is that it is not really effective so far as shutting out any of our oats at the present time is concerned, that there has been no hardship and no restriction has been necessary on the export of our oats. I thought I covered the point when I was on my feet before with reference to this being a hard and fast agreement for the first six months. We feel that if we can show cause, consideration will be given, just as they showed consideration in the extension of the first three months, because they do appreciate that we have tried in every way to cooperate with them. The number will be in the neighbourhood of 20,000 cattle on the basis of 1933. It was thought some two or three weeks ago, with the improvement of the situation in the old country, that there would be no necessity for restriction at all, but since then due to the conditions I have outlined the price has been depressed still further and things have not improved the way they had hoped.

While we were on the export basis the producer was producing, so that he did not get the high price for his butter; but as soon as we were off the export basis we were all consumers. This is where the tariff plays the trick, because the consumer pays the high price. So that when it is said that we are now enjoying a price of 30 cents for butter, the fact is that the intermediary gets the benefit; the producer did receive from 13 to 15 cents per pound during the producing season, and the consumer is paying the difference. Apparently there has not been the great success which the hon. member for East Middlesex claims has been achieved. The imperial conference has not proven to be such a great benefit to the farmer in connection with the exports of cheese. The home consumption in 1932-33 was down 7,548,392 pounds as compared with 1930-31. Our exports, the major part of which are to the British Empire, were down by over $5,000,000, while home consumption had decreased by over 7,500,000 pounds. It is not a very successful policy. And why was the home consumption of cheese less? It is because the people have no money to buy cheese. They eat bread without butter or cheese, just plain bread. They have no money to buy cheese. If the people had more money they would buy cheese and the farmers would be more prosperous; they would be happier.

Cocoa butter,
